the in situ NMR measurements show the following: (1) The ions move in and out of the carbon electrode during charge and discharge.
the in situ magnetic resonance images reveal that the ion adsorption is non-uniform, and the ion adsorption occurs preferentially at the pore walls, and not in the centre of the pores.
we have developed a new method to investigate in situ electrochemical double layer capacitors and have demonstrated the method by studying a standard capacitor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of the structure and dynamics of electrolytes in nanoporous carbon electrodes for electrochemical double-layer capacitor applications.
the investigation of the structure, dynamics, and reactivity of matter at the nanoscale.
the design, synthesis and application of functional materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ions in the electrolyte are confined within the pores of the activated carbon, with the ions being adsorbed onto the pore walls.
the ion dynamics in the nanopores of a working capacitor is not as straightforward as it was previously assumed.
the ion adsorption is not uniform over the surface of the electrode.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the in situ MRI experiments provide a direct visualization of the ion dynamics in a real electrochemical double-layer capacitor.
we have shown that the ions do not penetrate the carbon pores, but instead form a layer of ions on the surface of the electrode.
this is the first in situ imaging of an electrochemical double layer capacitor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, contrary to the common assumption, the ion dynamics inside nanoporous carbons cannot be described as diffusion.

the charge storage mechanism of nanoporous electrodes in electrochemical double-layer capacitor devices is not as simple as the classical model of a parallel-plate capacitor, but rather involves a more complex combination of processes, including ion diffusion and surface conduction, that are strongly dependent on the state of charge.

the ion dynamics in the nanoporous carbon electrodes are dominated by the adsorption/desorption of ions onto the electrode surface, with little evidence for the diffusion of ions through the nanopores.
